title: Triage of public API responses
question: Did information visible without an account cross an access boundary?
work: I checked the documented public behavior and tested whether seeing a service description also granted access to the operations it described.
evidence: One data set was already public by design. A separate service still required a client certificate for its protected operations.
limits: Neither observation established access to restricted records. I held both leads out of the proposed reports.
recommendation: Keep the public data contract explicit and test that protected operations continue to require credentials.

title: Browser permissions and private data
question: Could a page on another site actually read a signed-in user's data?
work: I compared cross-origin response headers with what each service returned and checked whether the request reached private content.
evidence: I found permissive cross-origin headers on responses that sent the browser to sign in.
limits: A redirect alone did not demonstrate a private-data read. I recorded that distinction in the findings.
recommendation: Only allow trusted sites that need access. Retest in a browser using a controlled account and a recognizable piece of test data.

title: Who should see a profile field?
question: Did two views of the same kind of profile apply the same privacy rules?
work: I compared the fields returned to the same account through two related views, checking which details each included.
evidence: One response included contact fields that its counterpart omitted. I documented the difference for review.
limits: The demonstration context left the origin of the records and the caller's intended permissions unresolved.
recommendation: Define the fields each role may see in one place. Verify both views with fictional profiles and accounts in separate groups.

title: A connection versus access to messages
question: What could a visitor actually receive after opening a real-time connection?
work: I compared a signed-out connection with one opened by a fresh test account and recorded the application's response to each.
evidence: The application denied the signed-out visitor. The signed-in account connected and received no messages.
limits: I saw no messages belonging to another account. An empty account also could not establish how membership was enforced for an active conversation.
recommendation: Check membership for each subscription. Repeat the test with an invited account and an uninvited one.

title: Resource ownership in a shared service
question: Could an account tell whether a resource outside its workspace existed?
work: I checked the ownership rules in a staging workspace and compared responses for inaccessible and nonexistent resources.
evidence: Both returned the same missing-resource response. Access to a known resource was scoped to its parent within the test workspace.
limits: The assessment used one account. Confirming isolation between independently controlled workspaces required a second.
recommendation: Repeat with two separately owned workspaces and check that each owner can use only their own resources.
